tier_reason: README 'Speed measurements' table shows HighwayHashAVX2 0.24 vs SipHash 1.26 cycles/byte at 1024 B and 0.95 vs 1.93 at 64 B, measured on a Xeon E5-2690 v3 with benchmark code in the repo (highwayhash/benchmark.cc + highwayhash/nanobenchmark.cc). The README omits flags, but the arXiv paper it links (1612.06257, Sec. 5) gives the compiler and exact flags, so all A criteria are met.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Patched GCC 4.9, 64-bit, flags -std=c++11 -O3 -march=haswell -fno-exceptions -fno-tree-vrp -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-strict-aliasing -fPIE (flags stated in the linked arXiv paper 1612.06257, Sec. 5; README says only 'patched GCC 4.9')
corrections.caveats: Compared against SipHash/SipTreeHash, not std::hash. Benchmark used a patched, non-public GCC 4.9 build (the paper notes unmodified GCC 6.3 gives ~10% lower throughput and GCC 4.8.4 ~3x slower code) on ~2014-era Haswell-EP hardware, and the GitHub repository is archived (last commit 2024-04-18), so the numbers do not reflect modern compilers or CPUs. The accompanying arXiv paper is a preprint, not peer-reviewed.

notes: All README numbers match; the derived 5.25x (1 KiB) and ~2x (64 B) ratios are correct, and the paper itself says 5.2-5.3x vs SipHash at 1 KiB. Repo is archived with Apache-2.0 license and 1,603 stars; metadata is accurate.

tier_reason: The README 'Comparisons' section gives the compiler, flags and CPU for all 10 platforms, plus the exact measurement loop (README inline code block using komihash/wyhash/XXH3_64bits calls), comparing against xxHash and wyhash. The timer helpers (TClock/CSystem) and the bulk-test code are not published, but the cycles/hash loop can be reproduced as given.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Averages over all 10 compiler/CPU combos (overhead excluded): komihash 5.34 7.2 cycles/hash (0-15b) and 8.6 (8-28b) vs wyhash_final4 13.5/18.0, XXH3_64 14.2/21.8, XXH64 10.2/15.0. That works out to ~1.9-2.1x fewer cycles than wyhash_final4, ~2.0-2.5x fewer than XXH3_64 and ~1.4-1.7x fewer than XXH64 on short keys (derived from page data). On 256,000-byte bulk hashing komihash (19.3-42.7 GB/s) is slower than XXH3_64 (28.0-68.4 GB/s) on all 10 platforms and slower than wyhash_final4 on 8 of 10 (derived from page data), so the advantage is specific to short/medium keys.
corrections.caveats: Never benchmarked against std::hash itself: the evidence is against best-in-class non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, wyhash), not the std::hash baseline. The numbers are the author's own, and the benchmark exists only as an inline README snippet that relies on unpublished timer helpers (TClock/CSystem); the bulk GB/s test code is not published. On bulk throughput komihash loses to XXH3_64 on every listed platform.

notes: Every quoted number is on the README. I tightened the ratio range (vs XXH3_64 on 8-28b it is ~2.5x) and made the bulk caveat more precise (XXH3_64 wins bulk on all 10 platforms, not just 'some'). Metadata is accurate: MIT, 286 stars, last commit 2026-08-04, not archived.

tier_reason: The README 'Scores' section states the CPU (i7-6700K), compiler (gcc 5.4.0) and CFLAGS (-march=native -O3 -fPIC). The numbers come from SMHasher, which is public (github.com/rurban/smhasher, which includes t1ha, as the README says), so tier A holds. The verdict is downgrade only because the claim was mislabeled and overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Small keys (1-31 bytes, avg cycles/hash): t1ha_aes 33.03 and t1ha 35.55 vs xxHash32 43.72, which is ~1.32x and ~1.23x fewer cycles (derived from page data). Large keys (262144-byte block, MiB/s): t1ha_aes 34,636.42 and t1ha 12,228.80 vs xxHash32 5,513.55, i.e. ~6.3x and ~2.2x (derived from page data), or ~3.1x and ~1.1x vs xxHash64's 11,123.15 MiB/s (derived from page data). The ~6.3x/~2.2x figures are bulk-throughput ratios, not small-key ones.
corrections.workload: SMHasher speed tests from 2016 on an Intel Core i7-6700K (README 'Scores' tables): average cycles/hash over 1-31-byte keys and bulk MiB/s on a 262144-byte block, comparing t1ha / t1ha_aes against xxHash32/64, Murmur2/3, FNV1a, CRC32/64-HW, MUM, City/Farm/Metro/Spooky and others.
corrections.baseline: xxHash32 (also xxHash64 and the Murmur2/Murmur3 family) in SMHasher speed tests
corrections.caveats: The benchmark data is from 2016 on a Skylake i7-6700K with GCC 5.4, and the exact SMHasher revision is not stated. The README's newer self-benchmark (make check, i7-4600U, GCC 9.3, flags unstated) shows t1ha2_atonce at 17.25 cycles/hash on 7-byte keys vs xxhash32 16.5, xxh3_64 15.1 and wyhash_v7 14.1, so t1ha2 is not faster on tiny keys against modern hashes; on 16 KiB keys t1ha2 (0.213 c/B) beats xxh3_64 (0.301) but roughly ties wyhash_v7 (0.206). The GitHub repo is an archived mirror: per the README, GitHub deleted the author's account in 2022, the repo was later restored read-only, and the origin moved to GitFlic. Compares against xxHash/Murmur, not std::hash.

notes: The record paired MiB/s values (which are the 262144-byte bulk column, identical in both tables) with a 'small keys' label, overstating the small-key speedup (real ~1.2-1.3x vs xxHash32). The license is confirmed Zlib from the LICENSE file (GitHub spdx is NOASSERTION); stars 367, last commit 2025-02-15 and archived (abandoned) are accurate. I could not check the GitFlic origin (request timed out), so its activity is unverified.

tier_reason: PR #25 shows edited search_test2 output (the benchmark code test/search_test2.cpp is in the mainline repo) timing std::search against boyer_moore_search and boyer_moore_horspool_search. It gives no compiler, flags, CPU or standard library, so the tier is C.

corrections.caveats: The quoted numbers come from PR #25, opened in 2016 by contributor Jeremy Murphy (jeremy-murphy), not Marshall Clow. The PR proposes a Musser-Nishanov searcher and is still open and unmerged. The timing rows used here are for the already-mainline boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool searchers. Compiler, flags, CPU model and standard library are not stated, and the author warns of 5-10% run-to-run variance, so treat the ~4-5x figures as indicative. The baseline is plain std::search; since C++17 the standard also ships std::boyer_moore_searcher and std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher (derived from these Boost searchers), which this PR does not compare against.
corrections.workload: Search a 2,756,252-entry random 8-bit corpus for a 105-entry pattern (middle), a 43-entry pattern (end) and a 91-entry pattern (not found), using boost::algorithm::boyer_moore_search / boyer_moore_horspool_search vs std::search, via Boost.Algorithm's test/search_test2.cpp.

notes: The numbers match the PR exactly (4.1x/4.5x middle, 5.6x not-found). The caveat misattributed the PR to Marshall Clow; its author is jeremy-murphy. last_commit on the default branch (develop) is 2026-08-05; 2026-08-12 is the repo pushed_at, not a default-branch commit. BSL-1.0, 131 stars and active status are all accurate.
